The hissing sound that is held in the back of the throat, and is held longer than other consonants, is known as a guttural fricative. Loanwords such as the word "bloke" meaning 'a man' in the mid-19th century, have been borrowed by mainstream English speakers from Shelta. There is no standard orthography for Shelta, and it can either be written following an Irish-type orthography or an English-type orthography. For example, the word for 'married' can either be spelled lósped or lohsped; the word for 'woman' can either be spelled beoir or byohr.

In the 19th century, the Lord's Prayer in Shelta showed a high Shelta lexical content, while the later Cant version showed a much lower Shelta lexical content. Both versions are adapted from Hancock who notes that the Cant reproduction is not exactly representative of actual speech in normal situations.

In 1980, the Supra received an upgrade in displacement with the 2.8-litre 5M-E engine. It was still a 12-valve SOHC engine, but had a power output of 116 hp (87 kW; 118 PS) and 145 lb⋅ft (197 N⋅m) of torque.

Hallucinations are sensory experiences that occur in the absence of any external stimuli. They can be auditory, visual, or tactile, and can involve seeing, hearing, or feeling things that are not actually present. Hallucinations can be associated with drug use, sleep deprivation, psychosis, neurological disorders, and delirium tremens. Many hallucinations happen also during sleep paralysis.

The version of the Lord's Prayer included in the 1662 revision of the Book of Common Prayer, was written by Bishop John Cosin for the coronation of King Charles I of Great Britain in 1625. During the Coronation of Charles III and Camilla in 2023, for the first time, the words were translated and also sung in Irish Gaelic, Scots Gaelic and Welsh.

Cranmer's sixth stanza, which mentions the Last Judgement and religious strife within Christendom ("the last dreadful day... strife and dissension..."), was a new addition, with no parallel in the Latin original or in Luther's version. The version included in the 1662 revision of the Book of Common Prayer compressed the content of the original seven verses into four (with a two-line doxology), but retained the Latin title. It was written by Bishop John Cosin for the coronation of King Charles I of Great Britain in 1625. The same words have been used at every coronation since, sung by the choir after the Creed and before the Anointing. The first verse is: Come, Holy Ghost, our souls inspire, and lighten with celestial fire.
